title: Button explains what will ‘keep Alonso going’ at Aston Martin
excerpt:
Jenson Button believes that Fernando Alonso’s re-signing with Aston Martin is hugely important for the team and, as long as he can see progress, that will “keep him going”.

At the end of September it was confirmed that 45-year-old Alonso would be continuing at Aston Martin, with the squad running an unchanged line-up of the Spaniard and Lance Stroll for 2027.

That latest deal will see the two-time World Champion – who won his titles two decades ago with Renault – compete in his 24th F1 season next year as the Silverstone-based outfit look to bounce back from a challenging 2026.

The team currently sit 10th in the Constructors’ Championship and required a B-spec update in Hungary to lift their performance level. However, even with that positive step, their engine supplier Honda have been off in terms of performance while reliability has also been a struggle.

However, Aston Martin still hold lofty ambitions for the future having also brought in the likes of Team Principal Adrian Newey in a bid to reach the top, and for 2009 F1 World Champion Jenson Button – an Aston Martin Ambassador – seeing signs of progress will be crucial in keeping Alonso involved with the project.

“I mean, there always has to be a little bit of doubt, because he's 45 years old now,” Button told F1.com when asked if there were any doubts Alonso would stick around. “I've been out of the sport for 10 years, and I retired because I was tired!

“I mean it always has to be a little bit of that, but it amazes me – his dedication and how much he loves competing at the top level, and he's still got it. So why not then keep going until he doesn't want it anymore?

“He is going to want to see progress, that is the main thing. He probably knows he's not going to win races any time soon, but as long as he can see progress and he is moving closer to that win, that’s what’s going to keep him going.”

Alonso credits 'phenomenal' car after strong drive in Brazil

‘I don’t know how he does it’

With Alonso and Aston Martin preparing for a fifth campaign together next year, it’s the latest chapter in a remarkable F1 career that began in 2001 with Minardi. Since then, he has gone on to represent the likes of Renault, McLaren and Ferrari while continuously operating at an elite level, with the Spaniard turning 46 midway through next season.

“I don't know how he does it,” Button continued. “I really don't. He lives racing, he lives F1. When he's not in an F1 car he's in a go-kart on his track or he's driving ex-DTM cars.

“He's always driving something, and that's his passion, and he likes driving on dirt as well. He keeps himself very busy with racing, and fair play to him.

“For me, it was great to retire from F1 to go and do other things. Also, I’ve got other things I want to do in life, but his dedication to motorsport is undeniable and I think unparallelled.”

When asked if he’s still operating at his best-ever level, Button responded: “I don’t think you can compare really because the sport’s changed so much. But he’s still putting in an unbelievable effort and also what he's achieving.

“It's funny with Fernando, because most drivers look very similar. If you put them all in the same kind of car, you wouldn't be able to tell who's who.

“With Fernando you tell immediately. He's up in the steering wheel and he's [doing these] little adjustments the whole time and it's great to have the talent of Fernando in the sport.”

‘It seems to work really well’

Alonso’s partnership with Aston Martin has often felt like an ideal match, particularly in 2023 when he scored eight podiums on his way to a P4 finish in the Drivers’ Championship. Even this year, given the struggles the team have faced, the fact the Spaniard has still amassed seven points is a credit to his never-ending determination.

For Button that’s also how it has felt, as he highlighted the importance of a team’s atmosphere in helping drivers excel.

“A few years ago, when they were getting podiums, it felt amazing,” Button recalled. “But now I think someone with his experience, this team has had world champions racing for them for quite a few years now, and I think it's an interesting brand for racing drivers.

“We love cars, it's got Aston Martin in the title – that’s nice – but to be fair it's more about the performance on track and the team of people you have around you. You need them to believe in you as well, and sometimes that doesn't happen with a team, and you see it time and time again with drivers jumping in cars.

“You know, they're the next big thing and then it doesn't work. You go somewhere else and then it works, so atmosphere is really important in making sure drivers feel comfortable and they can maximise their talents and skills. It seems to work really well, and [Alonso] seems at home.”

For that reason, when it was confirmed that Alonso would be sticking around with the team into next season, it served as an important boost for everyone involved in the project.

“I think that's really important for this team and continuity with both drivers is really important,” Button said, commenting on that announcement. “They've been through the rough and hoping for the smooth, and the feedback from both of them is really key.

“Fernando is obviously the one that's won the world championships, but Lance's feedback is also important. We need two drivers' feedback to enhance the car and [to make] a car that works for both drivers as well, you need that. That's when you're fighting for points.”

title: Our writers on Antonelli’s title success and what it means
excerpt:
It’s been a couple of weeks since Kimi Antonelli became the youngest World Champion in Formula 1 history, so now feels like a perfect time to reflect on exactly what his success means for both him and the sport.

We asked our writers Lawrence Barretto, Chris Medland and James Hinchcliffe to give us their thoughts on his record-breaking title…

Lawrence Barretto (F1 Correspondent & Presenter)

I first spent some proper time with Antonelli back in 2024 at Monza. It came just a day after he crashed on his FP1 debut but you wouldn't have known it. He'd already addressed it, learned from it and compartmentalised it. Admittedly, Mercedes had also just announced he would get his F1 debut the following year with the team, but the way he was handling everything was impressive.

He needed all that mental strength in his rookie year as he encountered a rollercoaster season that yielded some brilliant highs – such as three podiums – but also some painful lows, including scoring just one point across the entire European leg that culminated in boss Toto Wolff calling his performance at his home race in Monza "underwhelming".

Once again, Antonelli didn't let anything get him down. His close-knit family unit and inner circle of Mercedes team members whom he had bonded with since he joined the programme provided him with the bubble he needed to avoid spiraling, reset and go again in search of the immense potential they were convinced he had.

So, when Mercedes offered him a title-contending car for 2026, a year earlier than they had planned – and after a winter where he knuckled down and learned all the harsh lessons he'd been handed in 2025 – Antonelli seized his opportunity and never looked back.

As his more experienced team mate and title favourite George Russell toiled, Antonelli excelled. It's true that Antonelli didn't know what he didn't know regarding the enormity of fighting for the F1 title but all the evidence from the last two years proved he was made of special stuff – and it's still on him to deliver.

Nine Grand Prix wins, including stunning victories in Monza and Austin, showed just how good he is in just his second season. To win a title so quickly, and take the mantle from four-time World Champion Sebastian Vettel as the youngest ever champion, was remarkable. And he's not changed one bit from the charming, funny, kind and thoughtful guy I chatted to back in 2024.

Chris Medland (Special Contributor)

I don’t mind admitting I made some pretty poor predictions ahead of the 2026 season, but I definitely didn’t feel like I was being overly harsh on Kimi expecting a season of highs and lows. I had him down for a few wins and some real flashes of brilliance, but a lack of consistency up against Russell, who I thought would win the title.

It’s easy to point to the new generation of car as levelling the playing field, and in many ways it did as Russell had three years of ground effect experience when Antonelli made his debut, but Russell had also raced the previous generation of car and had adapted well already. For Antonelli to be so much stronger than his team mate this year should not be dismissed as just down to the regulations.

The step forward has been remarkable, but I think what really stands out is the way in which Antonelli has handled pressure. It barely seemed to affect him at any stage. He maximised his race result so often, and that did not drop even as he took the title. He said he was tense in Mexico City but the only time he wasn’t on it in the race was the final lap when he had to back off due to tears.

The records Antonelli has broken on his way to maiden title

He even erred on the more cautious side in wheel-to-wheel battles at first (think back to the Sprint in Canada) and then pushed the limits slightly more once he knew where the line was in the internal battle at Mercedes. He’s also raced others really well, too, taking a patient approach.

Antonelli was so good this year that he actually was rarely tested in terms of a high-pressure title battle or that many intense on-track fights, but the prospect of seeing him in both in future is exciting. He has so much developing still to do, and so much potential, that this genuinely feels like the beginning of a special career.

His race engineer Peter Bonnington said Antonelli can definitely match the likes of Lewis Hamilton and Michael Schumacher given his ability. That’s huge praise, but also depends on him being given another title-contending car next year. I really hope he gets it, because the idea of him fighting Hamilton, Max Verstappen and even Lando Norris – three other champions in three different teams – in 2027 is mouthwatering.

James Hinchcliffe (IndyCar Race Winner and Analyst)

With Antonelli’s podium in Mexico City, which he shared with Verstappen and Hamilton, we saw another record fall to the Italian. One that, barring some nearly unimaginable miracle, may never be beaten. Taking the crown of youngest World Champion from Vettel by over three years is a truly monumental feat. It’s the type of statistic that usually leads a list of career accomplishments that most could only dream of.

It really does feel like just the start for Antonelli. This did not feel like a flash in the pan type of performance. This wasn’t a ‘lucky’ year where everything fell his way. Yes, his Mercedes certainly started the year as the dominant package, but it’s what he did with it that was so impressive.

Antonelli still had to beat a much more experienced team mate in Russell. He had to out-qualify, out-race and overall outperform someone who went toe-to-toe with Hamilton and came out on top. He was placed in so many situations where it took more than just raw speed to win. It took good decision making. It took exceptional race craft. It took the kind of calm under pressure that simply can’t be taught.

In the same way that when Mercedes dominated the mid-teens, or Verstappen crushed the competition in the 2023 season, you could separate the driver’s accomplishment from the superior machinery. When you did that this season, some of Antonelli’s performances were simply sublime.

And Antonelli hasn’t had the best car all season. As the competition got better – got closer – he kept his cool and kept executing at a level that you’d expect from someone far his senior in both age and experience.

When you saw Hamilton’s early performances, when you saw Verstappen’s, you thought you were watching something special. And you were right. They went on to be the two most dominant drivers of their day. You get that same feeling watching Antonelli. It made the visuals from that Mexico podium all the more prophetic.

Pull up a chair. We’re witnessing greatness.

title: Piastri on his tough 2026 and why it could make him stronger
excerpt:
By his own admission, 2026 has been tough for Oscar Piastri. The season began with a DNS in front of his home crowd in Australia, was swiftly followed by another in China, and has brought with it significant challenges – particularly the task of getting to grips with McLaren’s MCL40.

While he currently sits a place behind team mate Lando Norris in the Drivers’ Championship, he is 94 points away from the Briton in seventh. Norris also has three wins this year, the most recent of which came last weekend in Sao Paulo, while Piastri has only been on the podium twice – and those were in rounds three and four of the campaign.

It’s a significant contrast to 2025 when the 25-year-old was embroiled in an intense three-way fight for the title that went all the way to the last race of the season, before Norris eventually triumphed and Red Bull’s Max Verstappen settled for second.

But the results do not tell the whole story of Piastri’s 2026 so far. While the change of regulations brought about an obvious reset in the pecking order – with Mercedes emerging as the class of the field to displace McLaren, who had won the last two Constructors’ Championships – there has also been a significant technical challenge for the Australian to overcome. It’s an exercise that has been far from straight forward.

‘It’s been tougher than I expected’

“It's been tough, definitely been tough,” Piastri admits to me as we catch up ahead of the United States Grand Prix in Austin. At this point he’s just come off a P5 result in Singapore and it looks like things are coming together again after a difficult first half of the year.

At the heart of his difficulties have been his struggles to adapt his natural driving style to the demands of McLaren’s MCL40 car. As mentioned by Team Principal Andrea Stella, Piastri has been unable to drive through “pure instinct” in certain conditions.

“As a team, we've not been as competitive as we would have wanted obviously and, I think for me, personally it's been tougher than I expected with trying to get to grips with the car,” the Australian continues.

“Obviously as a sport it's been a very demanding year in terms of getting used to the power units as well. It's definitely thrown in a lot of challenges, and I feel like I've had to change a lot of things in how I drive, or certainly tweak things.

“But I feel I'm making some progress now in the second half of this year, so yeah, just trying to continue that.”

McLaren’s drivers have both said at various points that the MCL40 is a difficult beast to tame, and it takes a lot to extract its full potential. But, for Piastri, that’s been coupled with having to retrain the driving instincts that have come so naturally to him over the last few years.

It’s no easy feat and, as any athlete will testify, when you’re having to think that intensely about the adjustments you need to make then it becomes increasingly hard to find your optimum performance level.

Piastri and management team mutually terminate agreement

“The biggest thing has probably been the general driving style you have, or that you need, is quite different for this year's car compared to previous years,” the 25-year-old explains.

“Even in previous years there's been an element of adaptation and learning for that – sure – but I think [it’s been a] combination of a few different things this year.

“Obviously, the cars are smaller, the tyres are quite different. It means you really have to drive the car on the edge all of the time – certainly our car, I don't know what others think of it.

“That's been quite different. You're always driving on the edge to an extent, but this year it's really always taking you beyond the edge of trying to salvage things.

“So, it's felt quite different to previous [cars] and even a lot of the previous cars I've driven in general. That's been quite an adaptation process and learning to trust the car and retrain what feels like the limit is never an easy thing to try and adapt. But hopefully I’m making progress.”

Without doubt Piastri is making that progress he is hoping for. Over the Singapore Grand Prix weekend, McLaren CEO Zak Brown said as much as he acknowledged the Australian was back to the driver he knew.

“He’s feeling more confident and on top of things,” Brown explained in the Team Principals’ Press Conference. “I like where both our drivers are now.”

While Piastri would perhaps rather have had another season fighting for titles, as he was in 2025, he does acknowledge that, in the long term, it might be a positive for him to have gone through the technical challenges that have been thrown at him this year.

“I think so,” he responds when I propose that line of thought. “You know, even some of the challenges from last year, they weren't completely dissimilar to what I've got this year, and I feel like I've definitely made a lot of progress on that in general.

“These last few races are definitely going to be another challenge in terms of testing where I'm at, in terms of developing those skills. Having that challenge has been tough, obviously, but getting through it, and then continuing to work on it, [is] ultimately going to be rewarding and [will] hopefully set me up for whatever car we get [in future].”

‘It's been good to see everybody pulling together’

Despite the way 2026 has panned out, with McLaren playing catch up following their back-to-back championship-winning years, the atmosphere within the squad is still positive.

Of course, part of the reason they began this season on the back foot was because last year’s drivers’ title went right down to the wire in the Abu Dhabi finale – Red Bull, after all, found themselves in the exact same position.

But as the year has gone on the team have found gains through development, one of their key strengths over the last few seasons, and Piastri insists they are as determined as ever to return to the top.

“It's been good to see everybody pulling together and this year has definitely been more challenging for sure,” says Piastri as I ask about the atmosphere within the squad. “I think everyone is still very determined to get back to where we know we can be.

Stella reveals how McLaren triumphed at Interlagos

“The competition [to Mercedes] is definitely going to step up in terms of, not just the competitiveness they have, but the continued development and stuff like that. They're raising the bar as well.

“I feel like we've set the bar pretty high in the last couple of years and that's the beauty of F1 – everyone is always pushing the boundaries further and further.

“I think we're on our way back there, development and upgrades have always been a strong point for us, and hopefully we can just keep pushing.”

There’s also plenty to be said about a team growing stronger in times of adversity, which Piastri is also seeing first hand. McLaren have, after all, roared back from difficult situations before.

“Definitely between myself, and the pretty close and intimate engineering team around me, we've learned a lot about each other and how we get the most out of ourselves [as well as] how we get more out of ourselves,” he explains. “So that's been a good process to go through for sure.”

‘I've always tried to remove results from what success looks like’

As is so often said in the intense world of F1, you live and die by the stopwatch. So, given Piastri and McLaren have not been able to deliver the results they both might have wanted, what has brought the Australian joy this year?

“I think trying to make progress,” he answers. “I've always tried to remove results from what success looks like.

“Of course, results do help. But especially when you're not in a position to win races, or whether it be because of the car or the kind of struggles I've had this year, sometimes a win and a successful weekend looks like improvement rather than perfection, is what I would say.

“That's brought me joy, for sure. There's been some very strong weekends this year that I've been really happy with. [I’m] just trying to work through those things.”

And what also comes as an additional challenge for drivers, when things aren’t going as well as hoped, is wrapping up your self-worth and identity entirely in F1 and what you do on the track.

“I mean, it is definitely a challenge because we spend so much time working at races and stuff like that,” Piastri adds. “It's definitely a challenge to be able to switch off from that.

“But I think outside of the track, I still enjoy the same things I always have – being able to spend time with my girlfriend, being able to have a few hours, a few days to kind of decompress, watch TV, play my simulator, play video games, whatever it might be. They're the same things that bring me joy, so yeah, that side of things hasn't changed.”

All you need to know about Oscar Piastri

Piastri has always been praised for that level-headed approach. It’s proved beneficial when fighting for titles, and it will absolutely be beneficial now as he seeks to turn around his fortunes.

Of course, what also helps is the strong sense of belief he has that McLaren will be back fighting for championships in the very near future.

“I certainly hope so,” he says. “I think it's been intriguing this year to see how things have ebbed and flowed.

“Everyone's kind of had their strong moments in terms of the top four teams. So yeah, we're pushing very hard to get back to that of course. Like I said, the teams around us have definitely raised the bar, but I know that we can raise it even higher.”

Whenever that time comes for McLaren, Piastri will have hoped he has raised his own bar just as high. And there’s every chance that the trials and tribulations of 2026 will have been crucial in helping him get there.

title: Antonelli names his biggest threat for 2027 title defence
excerpt:
Kimi Antonelli believes that Red Bull’s Max Verstappen will represent the greatest threat to his title defence in 2027, with the Italian anticipating a “very close fight” between the top teams.

Nine race wins and an additional seven podiums propelled Antonelli to the 2026 Drivers’ Championship, which he sealed with P3 in Mexico City behind former champions Verstappen and Lewis Hamilton.

Over the last two seasons, the Dutchman has garnered a reputation for remarkable comebacks – he missed out on the 2025 title by just two points, and has now stormed into second place thanks to Red Bull’s turnaround this year.

It’s no surprise, then, that the Mercedes driver picked him out as potentially his biggest rival for 2027.

Speaking in Italian during a press conference hosted by Sky Sport F1 Italia in his home town of San Marino, he said: “If I had to choose one driver, I'd say Max – he's the one who might cause the most problems.”

But Verstappen won’t be the only one hoping to challenge Antonelli, with Ferrari and McLaren likely aiming for more consistent performances at the front of the field.

Although both teams have clinched victories in 2026 (two for the Scuderia and three for McLaren’s Lando Norris), their form has fluctuated, opening the door for Red Bull to fight for better results and shake off their frustrating start to the latest era.

Add the refreshed teams' battle to George Russell’s desire to recover from his rollercoaster campaign and contend for his own maiden title, and 2027 is shaping up to be a tantalisingly competitive season.

"I think next year will be a very close fight among all of us, among all the top teams, because we are already very close,” Antonelli added. “Looking at Red Bull too, with all the upgrades they have brought, they have kept improving.

“McLaren had a period when they made huge gains, then a spell when they perhaps struggled more, but now they have bounced back. Ferrari [are] always there.

“It would be amazing to have a fight among all of us from the top teams, including Lewis, Charles [Leclerc], my team mate [Russell], Max and Lando. I think it will be a very close fight.”

title: Why are F1 drivers obsessed with padel?
excerpt:
Padel has become an increasingly popular sport among Formula 1 drivers, with Fernando Alonso and George Russell teaming up on the court, while Pierre Gasly has even invested in his own team. Now Aston Martin have taken that connection a step further with the launch of a new collection of padel rackets.

Padel has found a growing following within the paddock. But what exactly is the sport, and why have so many F1 drivers taken to it?

Aston Martin bring F1 to the padel court

Ahead of the 2026 United States Grand Prix,Aston Martin announced a collaboration with racket sports brand Padeltek, becoming the first F1 team to formally partner with a company specialising in padel and pickleball.

The collection features three padel rackets and accompanying cover bags, with pickleball equipment set to follow in 2027. To celebrate the launch, Aston Martin hosted an event in Austin, where Jenson Button, Jessica Hawkins, Jak Crawford and Pedro de la Rosa took to the court.

For Matt Chapman, Aston Martin's Head of Licensing and Merchandise, the sport's popularity within the paddock presented an opportunity to explore a new area for the team.

"Padel was a particularly interesting opportunity given its incredible growth and the natural connection it has developed with the Formula 1 paddock," Chapman told F1.com.

"We've seen how popular the sport has become among drivers and teams, but the appeal goes much further than that. It has a global and diverse community, which presents an exciting opportunity for us to connect with new audiences and explore a different side of our brand."

However, Chapman explained that the team wanted to ensure the collaboration went beyond simply adding its branding to existing equipment.

"Authenticity was really important to us from the outset. We wanted to create something that went beyond simply putting our name on a product, ensuring the collection genuinely reflected both our identity and the demands of the sport.

"Working with Padeltek allowed us to bring together their expertise in padel equipment, with our own design. We wanted the collection to feel unmistakably Aston Martin, while ensuring the products were designed to perform on court. Striking that balance between design, functionality and performance was key."

Aston Martin's Chief Marketing Officer, Rob Bloom, believes the competitive similarities between Formula 1 and padel have contributed to the sport's popularity.

"There's a natural crossover between the two sports, particularly when you consider the competitive mindset and the importance of quick thinking, precision and reaction times," Bloom told F1.com.

"Padel has become a sport that has brought people together, whether that's drivers, team members or fans, and it's become a great way for the paddock to connect away from the intensity of a race weekend."

What is padel, and why do F1 drivers love it?

Combining elements of tennis and squash, padel is typically played in doubles on an enclosed court surrounded by glass walls and fencing.

The scoring system is similar to tennis, but players serve underarm, use solid rackets and can return shots after the ball rebounds off the surrounding walls. The fast-paced rallies demand quick reactions, communication and teamwork, qualities that also play an important role in Formula 1.

According to Mike Dale, Editor of The Padel Paper, its accessibility is a major part of the appeal, particularly for professional athletes.

"Padel has indeed become really popular with current and ex-sportsmen and women. The sport is obviously very trendy and quite a lot of the emerging clubs are quite high-end, so the environment is attractive to people from the equally glamorous F1 world," he told F1.com.

"But the biggest reason is that padel is very easy to become quite good at quite quickly, particularly if you've got a baseline of athleticism, sporting ability and hand-eye coordination. And that feeling of being 'good' quite quickly is very addictive!"

The social element is another attraction for drivers, with Lando Norris, Oscar Piastri, Carlos Sainz, and Charles Leclerc among those regularly enjoying matches away from the track.

Ahead of the 2026 Singapore Grand Prix, Norris and Gabriel Bortoleto were spotted enjoying a game, while Alex Albon revealed that drivers had even established a group chat to organise late-night matches during the race weekend.

Despite taking place away from the pressures of a Grand Prix weekend, their competitive instincts remain.

Fernando Alonso has played padel for well over a decade, and during the 2023 Mexico City Grand Prix weekend revealed that he and Russell had enjoyed an unbeaten record together.

"I was [impressed by Russell]. I've been playing padel for, 12 or 15 years," Alonso said.

"But I think George is quite new to it and he was strong. And we are unbeatable at the moment! We play once and it's 100% dominant wins!"

Russell, meanwhile, explained that padel had become a welcome hobby during the latter stages of the season.

"Team mates on the padel court, 100% record against our competitors. It's always nice to do that as a sport, I've been getting into it a little bit as this year has progressed, and especially this time of the season, you spend a lot of time away, so it's nice to have a hobby on the side."

Piastri has also admitted that the drivers take their matches rather seriously.

"We take it far too seriously, yes. But it's very good fun and a good way of, you know, just keeping yourself awake."

Gasly takes his passion for padel further

While many drivers enjoy padel recreationally, Pierre Gasly has become involved in the sport as a team owner.

The Alpine driver is an investor in 10Padel, a team competing in the Hexagon Cup, an international padel competition which has attracted several high-profile investors.

"Padel is something I really enjoy in my daily life, and I believe it's a sport with incredible business potential," Gasly told Reuters in February 2026. "I'm happy to be a part of its growth through my team."

For Gasly, exploring interests outside Formula 1 is an important part of his life.

"Formula 1 opens many opportunities. While I wake up thinking about F1 and fall asleep thinking about it, there's more to life. I want to discover other things and mix them with my passions," he explained.

Could Formula 1 help padel reach new audiences?

With drivers regularly sharing their enthusiasm for padel and Aston Martin introducing its own equipment collection, the relationship between the two sports continues to develop.

For Aston Martin's Bloom, the partnership offers an opportunity to engage with fans beyond the traditional motorsport environment.

"Formula 1 has an incredibly diverse fanbase, and for Aston Martin, it's about finding authentic ways to meet fans on their terms – that means in their communities beyond motorsport. Padel is a great example of that.

"Collaborations like this allow fans to engage with the team through something they enjoy themselves, creating a connection that extends beyond the racetrack. Ultimately, we want to be part of the conversations and communities that matter to our fans, wherever their interests lie."

Dale similarly believes that partnerships involving F1 teams and drivers could help introduce padel to new audiences.

"These F1 and padel partnerships help raise padel's profile even more. There's a massive investor buzz around padel, with new clubs, tech, equipment and apparel being launched on a daily basis."

He also highlighted the influence of high-profile figures, including football legends David Beckham, Lionel Messi and Cristiano Ronaldo, in attracting potential players.

"When people see these celebrities on their social timelines holding a racket and smiling, it raises public awareness and curiosity about the game. It also makes it aspirational. 'If Beckham or Lando's doing it, I want to try it too!'"

Padel has also made appearances at Grand Prix venues, with courts installed at Silverstone in recent years and an area dedicated to the sport at the United States Grand Prix in Austin.

For fans tempted to follow their favourite drivers onto the court, Dale believes the ease of picking up the game is one of its greatest strengths.

"Almost anyone can go on court and have enjoyable rallies straight away – friends, families, all ages and abilities. You quite quickly get that magic feeling of 'I can do this!', which then equally quickly becomes, 'I'm good at this!' and that's very addictive."

With drivers competing against each other away from the track and teams beginning to get involved, padel is becoming an increasingly familiar part of life in the F1 paddock. And judging by the enthusiasm of those already playing, the competition is unlikely to remain confined to the circuit.

title: Toto Wolff's journey from Williams to nine F1 titles
excerpt:
After guiding Mercedes to a ninth Constructors' Championship, Toto Wolff has drawn level with Sir Frank Williams in the history books. Here is how the Austrian became one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses.

When Mercedes secured their ninth Constructors' Championship at the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix, it marked another significant milestone in the career of Team Principal Toto Wolff.

The result saw the Silver Arrows draw level with Williams on nine teams' titles, placing them behind only Ferrari and McLaren in Formula 1 history. For Wolff, the achievement carried particular significance given his beginnings in the sport.

Before overseeing Mercedes' record-breaking run of eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, the Austrian had made his first steps into Formula 1 management at Williams, working alongside the team's legendary founder, Sir Frank Williams.

Now, more than a decade after joining Mercedes, Wolff has matched Frank's tally of nine Constructors' titles, having guided the Brackley-based outfit back to the top following four seasons without championship success.

But how did a former racing driver and businessman become one of Formula 1's most successful team bosses?

A racing driver turned businessman

Born in Vienna in 1972, Wolff's motorsport career began behind the wheel rather than on the pit wall. After developing an interest in racing as a teenager, he competed in Austrian Formula Ford and claimed a class victory at the 1994 Nürburgring 24 Hours.

His racing career also included an appearance in the FIA GT Championship in 2004, although by this point, Wolff had already begun establishing himself in the business world, realising his talents lay beyond the cockpit.

He founded investment firms Marchfifteen in 1998 and Marchsixteen in 2004, with interests spanning technology and industrial businesses, while maintaining his connections to motorsport.

Those interests included HWA AG, the company responsible for Mercedes-Benz's DTM and Formula 3 programmes, providing Wolff with experience of the commercial and competitive sides of racing before entering Formula 1 management.

Finding his feet at Williams

Wolff's involvement in Formula 1 began in 2009 when he invested in Williams, a team already established as one of the most successful in the sport's history.

Founded by Sir Frank Williams and Sir Patrick Head, the outfit had won nine Constructors' Championships between 1980 and 1997, enjoying success with drivers including Nigel Mansell, Alain Prost, Damon Hill and Jacques Villeneuve.

Although Williams were no longer regularly challenging for titles when Wolff arrived, the Austrian developed a close relationship with Frank, eventually becoming the team's Executive Director in 2012.

Reflecting on their relationship in a 2020 interview with F1.com, Wolff recalled the moment they first met.

"Frank Williams is an incredible person, with an aura and charisma that very few people in Formula 1 possess. I was lucky enough to meet him personally in 2009, and I'll never forget the first thing he said to me: 'I heard you can help me repay my mortgage!'"

Wolff's time at Williams would prove relatively brief, however, as another opportunity emerged in 2013.

A new chapter with Mercedes

In February 2013, Wolff joined Mercedes as Managing Partner, acquiring a 30% stake in the Formula 1 operation and taking on wider responsibilities for the manufacturer's motorsport activities. The move placed him alongside three-time World Champion Niki Lauda and Team Principal Ross Brawn as Mercedes continued building towards the front of the grid.

Wolff's first season coincided with Lewis Hamilton arriving at Mercedes to join Nico Rosberg, beginning one of the most successful partnerships in the sport's history.

Mercedes secured three victories during the 2013 campaign, with Rosberg winning in Monaco and Great Britain before Hamilton took victory in Hungary. The team eventually finished second in the Constructors' Championship behind Red Bull.

However, the introduction of new turbo-hybrid power unit regulations in 2014 would transform the competitive order.

Mercedes won 16 of the season's 19 Grands Prix, while Hamilton secured his second Drivers' Championship after a season-long battle with Rosberg. The result also delivered the team's first Constructors' title.

It was the beginning of an unprecedented period of success.

Eight consecutive championships

Mercedes' dominance continued throughout the following seasons, as Wolff oversaw a team that established a new benchmark for consistency in Formula 1.

Hamilton added further Drivers' Championships in 2015, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2020, while Rosberg defeated his childhood friend and team mate to claim the 2016 crown. And while despite the intense rivalry between their drivers, Mercedes maintained their position at the front, navigating regulation changes and challenges from Ferrari and Red Bull.

By 2021, the Silver Arrows had won eight consecutive Constructors' Championships, a record unmatched by any other Formula 1 team.

Although Hamilton narrowly missed out on an eighth Drivers' title to Max Verstappen that season, Mercedes secured another teams' crown, extending their extraordinary run of success.

A ninth title and a place alongside Frank Williams

Mercedes' remarkable winning streak ended in 2022, as the introduction of new ground effect regulations changed the competitive landscape and left the team struggling to match their rivals.

For Wolff, it marked the beginning of a challenging period, with Mercedes managing just five Grand Prix victories across the following four seasons. Despite the setbacks, the Austrian remained at the helm, overseeing changes to the team's driver line-up and preparations for another major regulation overhaul in 2026.

Hamilton's departure for Ferrari at the end of 2024 also marked the conclusion of one of Formula 1's most successful driver-team partnerships, with Wolff choosing to promote young Italian Kimi Antonelli alongside George Russell.

"I made up my mind five minutes after Lewis Hamilton told me that he's going to Ferrari," said Wolff following Antonelli's announcement in August 2024.

"That is the line-up with these two [Russell and Antonelli] that I always wanted, bearing in mind the fast-tracking that we did with Kimi and everything related there too, but that was immediately what I wanted to do."

The decision represented a significant show of faith in the then 18-year-old, who had progressed through Mercedes' junior programme before making his Formula 1 debut in 2025.

“Wolff's decision was vindicated in 2026, with Antonelli securing his maiden Drivers' Championship at the Mexico City Grand Prix, becoming the youngest World Champion in F1 history at just 20 years old.”

Mercedes' resurgence was completed at the following round in Sao Paulo, where Russell and Antonelli's fourth and fifth-place finishes secured the team's ninth Constructors' Championship, ending a four-year wait for another title.

The achievement marked Mercedes' ninth Constructors' Championship, their first since 2021, and brought Wolff level with Sir Frank Williams, whose nine titles had been won across the 1980s and 1990s.

Speaking to Sky Sports following the race, Wolff reflected on the significance of matching the man who had helped him establish his career in Formula 1.

"Obviously, Frank is such an unbelievable icon of the sport, and to be tied on constructors' championships, I never thought that was ever possible.

"I had a close relationship with Frank, and to be there, it's amazing. I can't believe it."

title: F1 ACADEMY Champion Palmowski graduates to Formula Regional

Additionally, the 20-year-old will join the Red Bull Junior Team next year and will benefit from a comprehensive testing programme, alongside continued support and development through the Red Bull Junior Programme and backing from F1 ACADEMY.

Ahead of next season, Palmowski will also get behind the wheel for the 2027 Race of Champions New Zealand in January, partnering up with 13-time Formula 1 race winner David Coulthard as part of Team GB.

Susie Wolff, Managing Director of F1 ACADEMY, commented: “What a journey it’s been for Alisha. From joining us as a Wild Card Driver in 2024 to becoming F1 ACADEMY Champion just two years later, she has grabbed this opportunity with both hands. Six defining moments on Palmowski's journey to becoming the 2026 F1 ACADEMY Champion

title: Mercedes' incredible history of Formula 1 success
excerpt:
After Mercedes secured their ninth Constructors' Championship in 2026, F1.com looks back at the Silver Arrows' remarkable history, including Juan Manuel Fangio's early success, their record-breaking run of eight consecutive titles and their return to the top of Formula 1.

Mercedes have written their name into the F1 history books once again by clinching a ninth constructors' crown, their points at the 2026 Sao Paulo Grand Prix returning them to the top of the sport for the first time in five years.

George Russell and Kimi Antonelli's fourth and fifth-place finishes at Interlagos were enough to seal the teams' title, just one week after the young Italian claimed his maiden Drivers' Championship in Mexico.

The achievement puts Mercedes level with Williams on nine constructors' titles, behind only Ferrari's 16 and McLaren's 10, and adds another chapter to a remarkable history that stretches back more than seven decades.

Their success began on track long before Lewis Hamilton, Nico Rosberg and the modern Mercedes team won eight consecutive Constructors' Championships though, that period between 2014 and 2021 one of the most dominant in F1 history...

The Silver Arrows' early success

Mercedes' history in Grand Prix racing dates back well before the Formula 1 World Championship was established in 1950, with the famous Silver Arrows enjoying considerable success during the 1930s.

The German manufacturer made its World Championship debut at the 1954 French Grand Prix, with Juan Manuel Fangio and Karl Kling securing a one-two finish in their first race behind the wheel of the Mercedes W196.

Fangio went on to win four races for Mercedes that season, securing his second Drivers' Championship, before returning in 1955 to claim another title alongside team mate Stirling Moss. The following campaign saw Mercedes win five of the six World Championship Grands Prix in which they competed, including a famous victory for Moss at the British Grand Prix – the first of his 16 career wins.

However, Mercedes withdrew from motorsport at the end of 1955 following a season overshadowed by the Le Mans disaster, in which driver Pierre Levegh and more than 80 spectators lost their lives. The decision brought an early end to the manufacturer's first period of F1 success, with Mercedes having claimed two Drivers' Championships in just two seasons. The Constructors' Championship would not be introduced until 1958.

Mercedes eventually returned to F1 as an engine supplier during the 1990s, initially partnering with Sauber before beginning a successful relationship with McLaren, where drivers Mika Hakkinen and Lewis Hamilton would go on to win titles with Mercedes power.

But it would take until 2010 for the manufacturer to return to the grid as a full works team.

A new era of Mercedes dominance

After Brawn GP's remarkable championship-winning campaign in 2009, Mercedes purchased the Brackley-based outfit and returned to Formula 1 with seven-time World Champion Michael Schumacher and Nico Rosberg as their drivers.

The team's early seasons brought mixed results, although Rosberg secured Mercedes' first victory as a works team since 1955 at the 2012 Chinese Grand Prix.

The arrival of Hamilton in 2013 marked another significant moment, with the Briton joining Rosberg as Mercedes prepared for major changes to Formula 1's technical regulations.

When the turbo-hybrid era began in 2014, Mercedes emerged as the team to beat. Winning 16 of the season's 19 Grands Prix, Hamilton and Rosberg dominated the championship, with the former claiming his second drivers' title as Mercedes secured their first constructors' crown.

It was the beginning of an extraordinary run.

They repeated the feat in 2015, once again winning 16 of 19 races, before taking their dominance to another level in 2016, claiming 19 victories across 21 Grands Prix. That year also brought one of the sport's most memorable intra-team rivalries, with Rosberg defeating Hamilton to secure his maiden World Championship before announcing his retirement just days later.

Valtteri Bottas joined Mercedes for 2017, helping the team continue their winning streak alongside Hamilton, who added four consecutive drivers' titles between 2017 and 2020.

In their time together, Hamilton claimed six drivers' titles, Rosberg added another, and Mercedes established themselves as one of the most successful outfits the sport had ever seen.

Even when Max Verstappen ended their run of drivers' crowns in 2021, Mercedes maintained their advantage in the teams' standings.

By the end of that year, Mercedes had achieved something no other team in F1 history had managed – eight consecutive Constructors' Championships.

But major regulation changes in 2022 would bring an end to their reign.

Returning to the top in 2026

The introduction of new ground-effect regulations in 2022 proved challenging for Mercedes, who struggled to replicate their previous dominance.

Russell secured the team's only victory of that season in Sao Paulo, while 2023 marked their first winless campaign since 2011. And whilst the Silver Arrows returned to winning ways in 2024, claiming four victories, they finished fourth in the standings.

The departure of Hamilton to Ferrari at the end of that year also marked the conclusion of the most successful driver-team partnership in Formula 1 history, with the seven-time World Champion having secured 84 Grand Prix victories for Mercedes.

In his place came the then 18-year-old Italian Antonelli, who partnered Russell for the 2025 campaign. The team finished second in the standings that year, setting the stage for another major opportunity as the sport prepared to introduce new technical regulations for 2026.

Just as they had done in 2014, Mercedes capitalised on the changes.

Russell opened the 2026 season with victory in Australia, before Antonelli secured his maiden win in China and quickly established himself as a championship contender.

By the time the paddock arrived in Brazil, Mercedes had claimed 12 Grand Prix victories from 19 Grands Prix, with Antonelli having already secured the Drivers' Championship in Mexico.

Their ninth teams' title followed at Interlagos, completing another championship double and making Mercedes the third-most successful constructor in the sport's history, level with Williams.

For Team Principal Toto Wolff, who has overseen all nine of Mercedes' Constructors' Championships – an achievement that sees him equal Sir Frank Williams' record for the most titles as a team boss – the win carries particular significance after four challenging seasons.

"We've taken a few years to be back on the top spot. Not many teams have been able to come back from such a situation.

"And it just shows that, you know, the great work, the great people that we have in our organisation. And it's fantastic to be among them."

More than 70 years after Fangio first tasted championship success with Mercedes, the Silver Arrows have once again established themselves at the summit of Formula 1.

title: Why the F1 driver market might produce one last twist
excerpt:
On paper, the news Racing Bulls will keep both Liam Lawson and Arvid Lindblad for next season leaves just one spot to be confirmed, but there's still the possibility of a change in one other seat on the grid...

So what's up for grabs in that one spot yet to be confirmed?

A seat at American squad Haas. Ollie Bearman is the incumbent and is going to be in it next year – they just haven't nailed down the details of the contract.

The Briton and Ferrari junior is in his second full season with Haas and currently sits in 13th place in the drivers' standings on 23 points.

He's levelled up in his second campaign, both in terms of Qualifying pace and racecraft – with the 21-year-old pulling off some particularly impressive overtakes.

Haas certainly want to keep him – so it's just a case of his management, Haas boss Ayao Komatsu and Ferrari boss Fred Vasseur coming to an agreement.

While it is a no-brainer for all parties to continue, the terms of the deal are important as Bearman will know that if Lewis Hamilton keeps delivering, he won't be leaving Ferrari anytime soon and that means there's no space for the Briton to move up.

And while Haas is a great place to be for Bearman for now – and his full focus is taking the team forward and helping them achieve the first podium in their history – he also knows he can't stay there forever if he wants to progress his career.

Watch this space, but it's certainly a case of when, not if, a deal is done for 2027.

'We see huge potential' – Komatsu on choosing Camara for Haas

Okay, that finalises the grid – so what's this about a possible change?

Well, this is where we turn our attention to Cadillac. When Sergio Perez and Valtteri Bottas signed with the newcomers ahead of this campaign, they both agreed multi-year deals.

These multi-year deals had options which needed triggering to confirm the second season in 2027.

Ahead of the Mexico City Grand Prix, Cadillac announced Perez had signed an extended deal keeping him at the team until at least the end of 2029.

A subsequent announcement about Bottas has yet to be released, with the team's American reserve driver Colton Herta linked with the seat that would offer him his F1 debut.

Herta has struggled in F2 and sits 19th in the standings, but the 26-year-old has impressed when behind the wheel of a Cadillac in FP1 sessions and the American team are keen to run an American driver on merit.

By taking part in the opening practice session in Brazil, Herta secured the final point needed for his Super Licence, clearing the way for a potential F1 drive.

Cadillac now have to decide whether they want to give him a debut next year or stick with 37-year-old 10-time Grand Prix winner Bottas alongside Perez.

What about one-time Grand Prix winner Esteban Ocon?

Given Haas are set to sign Bearman and Cadillac will have Bottas or Herta, it means there is no space on the grid for Ocon, who made his F1 debut back in 2016.

Earlier this month, Haas announced that Ocon would not complete the season with the team, which he was set to leave at the end of the year anyway.

Ocon – who has won one Grand Prix, taken four podiums and scored 490 points in 198 starts – has unfinished business with F1 and wants to find a way back in.

Initially, that will have to be a reserve role at best and with his experience in F1, it's believed he does have options for 2027.

title: Oscar Piastri dismisses F1 title collapse link to ongoing McLaren woes
excerpt:
Oscar Piastri does not believe his collapse in the 2025 F1 title race is linked to his ongoing struggles in the 2026 season.

Following his last victory to date in the 2025 Dutch Grand Prix, Piastri held a 34-point lead over team-mate Lando Norris and a 104-point advantage over Max Verstappen, with seven rounds remaining.

However, a crash in qualifying in Azerbaijan was the start of a poor run of form, with the Australian jumping the start in Baku before crashing on the opening lap, before expressing fury in Singapore after being barged past by Norris at Turn 2 on the first lap.

Then, in the United States, Piastri was generally held responsible for triggering a first-corner shunt in the Sprint that also eliminated Norris, before crashing out of the Sao Paulo Sprint.

In the Singapore-United States-Mexico City-Sao Paulo leg, Piastri finished fourth once and fifth three times, as Norris and Verstappen hit top form, with Piastri's fifth in Mexico coming as Norris won to climb to the top of the standings.

Piastri and Norris were then disqualified in Las Vegas for plank wear, with McLaren's strategy faux pas in Qatar then meaning an easy win became second to Verstappen as Norris ultimately won the title on 423 points, with Verstappen in second on 421 and Piastri third on 410, having led the table for 15 of the 24 rounds after a fast start, which included five wins in the first nine races.

In 2026, Piastri has claimed just two podium finishes all season, and has not finished in the top three since the Miami Grand Prix, with an average finishing place of 7.1 in the 16 races since, with Norris claiming three victories in a difficult MCL40 machine.

McLaren boss Andrea Stella has put Piastri's struggles down to his inability to adapt quickly to the new way the 2026 cars must be driven, with lack of downforce meaning the cars are subject to constant micro-corrections, something opposed to Piastri's uber-smooth driving style.

Reflecting on a tough season, Piastri explained that as far as he was concerned, his 2025 collapse has had no impact on his 2026 woes - and that he is "under no illusions" at the scale of the challenge in recapturing his best form.

"I'll be using the off-season to have a bit of a reset, have a bit of a rethink, and [having] a clear start is going to be useful," Piastri told the Up to Speed podcast.

"I don't think these problems are going to solve themselves in an off-season without putting a lot of effort into it, so there's definitely going to be a lot of hard work involved.

"The cars will evolve. The regulations are changing a little bit again next year, and we have to see what kind of tyres we have next year, because that can also make a difference.

"I'm under no illusion that it's magically going to be different next year. But I think, honestly, in some ways, last year going the way it did, I think if it had gone better last year, it would have made this year even more painful.

"I think a lot of the struggles this year, or all the struggles this year, are unrelated to what happened last year. It's been a separate issue, and this year has definitely taught me a lot. I feel like I'm getting on top of some of these struggles.

"Maybe not as consistently as I would like at the moment, but I think even Brazil qualifying didn't go to plan. But actually, the pace I had in the race was the strongest I've had for a long time. So, there are definitely signs of positives there.

"It is definitely one of those things where I'm going to have to go and grab it and pull things in the direction I want rather than hoping things come to me naturally."

[Article continues below]

Piastri continues on title collapse

When then asked why his title challenge had unravelled towards the end of the season, Piastri indicated he would do certain things "differently."

"[It was] for a number of reasons, really," he began.

"I think there were a couple of places where I just struggled for pace, and I think again some of those specifics are also present this year. I think also as a team we would definitely do some things a bit differently if we did it again.

"The impact of some of those things was big sometimes. And again, I think as a team we know what we would do differently if we were in that position this year.

"We've not had to worry about that because that's not the position we've been in. But I think some things would be done differently."

title: Colton Herta explains how 'piggyback' routine is aiding his F1 bid
excerpt:
Colton Herta has explained how racing for Hitech in Formula 2 while being based at Cadillac's Silverstone facility is sharpening his preparations for a potential F1 seat.

The American, who doubles as Cadillac's official test driver, moved into F2 this season specifically to close the gap on the 40 superlicence points required to race in Formula 1.

Whilst he did not achieve the results required to earn his superlicence through his championship position, he sits in 19th place with 26 points, with two rounds remaining.

However, through six FP1 outings for Cadillac, Herta earned enough points to finally qualify for the licence, with his run in Sao Paulo bringing him to his 40th point - meaning he can legally race in F1 in 2027, should Cadillac opt to promote him.

Herta's rookie F2 campaign with Hitech, however, has fallen well short of the top-10 finish in the standings that Cadillac CEO Dan Towriss had set as a target, and the 26-year-old has indicated he has no appetite for a second season in the category.

But the 2026 programme was never only about results. Hitech's Silverstone base sits close to Cadillac's own facility at Silverstone, and Herta has used that proximity to move between the two outfits throughout the year.

[Article continues below]

Herta - 'You're noticed'

Asked whether the switch from F2 to F1 remained the right career route, Herta pointed to the practical benefits of racing on the same weekends and circuits as the sport he is targeting.

"There are a lot of positives to the series," he said, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, following his FP1 outing at the Circuit of the Americas at the United States Grand Prix.

"You run on the same race weekends, so you kind of understand the flow of what the sessions look like."

Jokingly, he then added: "What I've experienced this year, you get to understand how bad traffic is to Formula 1 races and how early and late you have to leave."

Returning to the serious nature of the topic, he continued: "But I think it's important because you're here and you're noticed.

"You're in the eyes of the Formula 1 teams, and they see first-hand what you can do. You're running on the same race tracks that you will be racing on, which is a big one, and it's the main reason why I came over to do it.

"You're just immersed in it. I live in the UK, I'm in the shop every day [at Hitech], and they're right next to the F1 shop, so I can kind of piggyback back and forth, and I think it's important from that aspect.

"It makes the transition easier than coming from, say, IndyCar, sports cars, or whatever. So there are positives."

Sergio Perez has been retained by Cadillac, but Valtteri Bottas's seat still has not been confirmed, with Herta eyeing up the position, with Cadillac long making clear that fielding an American driver is a priority - but whether it is Herta remains an open question.

title: Toto Wolff reveals when he knew Kimi Antonelli would win 2026 F1 title
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has revealed when he started to realise that Kimi Antonelli would be crowned the youngest F1 champion in history.

Antonelli claimed the title in Mexico City on November 1st aged 20 years, 2 months, 7 days, to beat Sebastian Vettel's record from 2010 of 23 years, 4 months, 11 days by 3 years, 2 months, 4 days.

His triumph came after a successful campaign, which included nine race wins before the title, with no other driver having more than three, including a record-breaking five successive wins in China, Japan, Miami, Canada, and Monaco.

This run was the first time in history that a driver took their first five grand prix wins in succession, with Antonelli becoming the youngest driver to also record a grand chelem with his dominance in Monte Carlo.

Reflecting after the Italian's success, Wolff revealed that it was around the time of the Monaco win that he began to realise that Antonelli, who held a 66-point lead in the championship over Lewis Hamilton following the race in the Principality, would become the first Brackley driver to be crowned champion since Hamilton in 2020.

"I am so bad at remembering which race I thought he was going to do it, Wolff told media, including RacingNews365.

"I think there was no particular moment, but it was when he was able to put together race weekend after race weekend after race weekend, and how many consecutive races did he win?

"Five. Eventually, I knew that if we were able to provide him with the car, he was going to win the championship."

[Article continues below]

Not a "one-time wonder"

Recalling what he wants to achieve with Antonelli in the future, Wolff declared his intention to ensure the 36th F1 champion was not a "one-time wonder."

"What I've said to him is that together, we have to try for you to stay relevant all your life," Wolff said.

"You have 25 years to go because you're going to drive longer than anybody else did before, and I want to look back in many years and say: 'You stayed relevant all your life,' and that he isn't a one-time wonder.

"But we will work together in a way to help him improve where he can improve, get better and there are not many [drivers] that have stayed relevant, and also world champions who stayed relevant.

"That is what I want to achieve with him."

title: Lando Norris explains McLaren F1 trade-off in 'impossible dream' pursuit
excerpt:
Lando Norris has explained how McLaren elected to trade off the 2026 season in pursuit of the 2025 world championship titles.

McLaren successfully defended its constructors' title in 2025 as Norris became the first drivers' champion for the team since Lewis Hamilton in 2008, after a thrilling end to the season where Max Verstappen was hunting him down.

The team was forced to divert attention away from its 2026 preparations for the all-new chassis and power unit regulations to ensure Norris, or Oscar Piastri, got over the line, which Norris ultimately did by just two points from Verstappen.

Teams like Mercedes and Ferrari, who were not in the championship fight, were able to abandon their 2025 projects early, and will finish one-two in the championship, with McLaren engaged in a battle for third with Red Bull - which is currently in favour of Verstappen and Isack Hadjar.

Teams successfully defending their titles through major regulation changes is rare, with McLaren and Ferrari failing in 2009, and Mercedes also doing so in 2022 when the change to ground effects halted the team's run of eight consecutive constructors' crowns.

Reflecting on McLaren's season, outgoing drivers' champion Norris explained that given the scale of the regulation changes, hoping McLaren could win across eras was "an impossible dream" - especially as it traded off 2026 to ensure 2025 was successful.

"I don't think we've done many things badly this season," Norris reflected to media, including RacingNews365.

"I think we knew at the beginning of the season there was a big challenge ahead of us because of coming into a new regulation after last season, and generally that is a good part of it.

"I think we've actually had a very successful season in terms of catching up to our competition after starting easily over a second off compared to Mercedes and other teams.

"For us to catch up, I think you can easily see it more as a success than a failure, and I certainly don't want to look at this year as if it has been a failure because we won two seasons in a row, and I think to win a third in a row was a very high expectation.

"To win it in one of the biggest regulation changes ever, I think, was almost an impossible dream because you're not able to do everything at once: you're not able to fight for a world championship last year and fight for every last upgrade and bit of performance, and to come into this season just as confident.

"It is just impossible to have, so the compromise was this season to win the world championship last season - and that's one we'll continue to make."

title: Adrian Newey sees echoes of Red Bull's troubled past in Aston Martin
excerpt:
Adrian Newey can see certain "parallels" between his starts at Red Bull and Aston Martin.

Adrian Newey has said he recognises striking similarities between the state of Aston Martin when he joined and the condition of Red Bull when he first arrived there more than two decades ago.

Newey, now Aston Martin's team principal, made the comparison while speaking to media, including RacingNews365, at the United States Grand Prix at the Circuit of the Americas.

Red Bull bought the struggling Jaguar operation from Ford in late 2004, with Christian Horner installed as team principal before Newey arrived in early 2006.

Aston Martin, formerly Force India, has undergone its own extensive restructuring since Lawrence Stroll's takeover in 2018, including the departure of long-time team boss Otmar Szafnauer, a brief spell under Martin Whitmarsh, and the subsequent appointment of Andy Cowell.

Technical leadership at the Silverstone-based squad has also shifted repeatedly, with technical director Dan Fallows departing as Enrico Cardile and Newey were brought in alongside him.

It is against that backdrop that the 66-year-old designer drew the comparison between his two biggest career projects.

"I think there are actually a lot of parallels between when I started at Red Bull and when I started at Aston Martin," said Newey.

"Both teams, through their history, had had quite a lot of turmoil, with changes of owners, changes of senior managers, etcetera.

"And it's then really trying to get everybody working together, trying to break down silos, improve the culture, and that's been the same again."

[Article continues below]

Newey sees signs of progress

Aston Martin currently sits 10th in the constructors' championship with a miserly seven points after 20 grands prix following a tough campaign with new power unit supplier Honda.

The Japanese manufacturer's PU has struggled through its first season back as a full works partner, qualifying for the FIA's concession framework after falling more than four per cent behind the leading manufacturer, Red Bull-Ford, on combustion metrics.

Upgrades introduced at Zandvoort and Madrid have brought mixed results, with turbo lag and driveability issues persisting into the back end of the campaign.

Newey has insisted, however, that both his team and Honda are slowly coming together.

"I think we're making huge amounts of progress," said Newey. "It really feels now like the team's coming together.

"The team spirit within the engineering offices, in particular, is very strong now. I see a lot of ideas being generated, lots of people chatting with each other, working late in the evening.

"So, very impressed with how the individuals are really kind of… you can feel the buzz in the factory now.

"Honda, obviously, is working hard. They're a great company, as we all know, capable of great things, as they've proved many times in the past. We are working closely with them, and so I'm hopeful for the future."
