title: Mercedes continue march up F1 ladder as painful five-year wait ends
excerpt:
Mercedes now has just two F1 rivals ahead of it in terms of holding the most constructors' titles after regaining its crown for the first time since 2021.

After its fourth and fifth in the São Paulo GP, the team regained its crown for the first time since its record-breaking run came to an end in 2021, with Kimi Antonelli and George Russell combining to bring a ninth star to Brackley.

Mercedes has now won nine of the 13 constructors' titles up for grabs in the turbo hybrid era, with its engines also powering McLaren's glory in 2024 and 2025, meaning all but two constructors' titles since 2014 have been Mercedes-powered: these being Red Bull in 2022 and 2023.

Mercedes' ninth title now means it is equal third with Williams on nine titles, with only Ferrari and McLaren ahead of the Silver Arrows.

In total, just 15 teams have won the constructors' championship since it was introduced in 1958, with 'Team Brackley' responsible for 11 of those.

Mercedes originally started life as Tyrrell, which took the title with Jackie Stewart and Francois Cevert in 1971, before a spell as BAR and Honda failed to yield a title, before the famous 2009 success as Brawn GP.

Brawn then sold up to Mercedes for 2010, with this team being the one to claim the nine titles.

title: Isack Hadjar uses Lewis Hamilton to dismantle contentious F1 myth
excerpt:
Isack Hadjar has pushed back against the idea that modern F1 machinery and simulator technology make it easier for rookies to adapt to the championship, arguing that raw talent has always shone through regardless of era.

The Red Bull driver, who completed his first full season in 2025, was asked about the theory that today's generation of drivers benefits from tools unavailable to their predecessors.

Hadjar rejected the premise outright, pointing to Fernando Alonso and Lewis Hamilton as evidence that immediate adaptation has never been exclusive to the current crop.

Kimi Antonelli has been crowned F1 drivers' champion in just his second F1 season, but that is a feat matched in the modern era by Hamilton, who won his maiden title with McLaren in 2008 after arriving the previous year.

Jacques Villeneuve pulled off the same trick even earlier, claiming the 1997 championship with Williams in only his second campaign.

Asked whether simulators and improved car characteristics have flattened the learning curve for newcomers, Hadjar was unequivocal.

"I believe that if you're good, you're good," the Red Bull driver told media, including RacingNews365.

"You take Fernando [Alonso], Lewis [Hamilton]... Kimi [Antonelli] is a world champion, and you take the champions previously; they adapted quickly."

[Article continues below]

Further evidence to support his claim

Hadjar leaned more heavily on Hamilton's case, pointing to the Briton's explosive rookie campaign at McLaren in 2007, when he fought team-mate Alonso and Ferrari's Kimi Raikkonen for the title from his very first race.

"You saw what Lewis did in his rookie year," Hadjar added. "I think if you have the ability, it doesn't really matter the car.

"What we see compared to probably 20, 30 years ago is the number of drivers that adapt quickly.

"I think just the quality and the competitiveness you see in junior categories maybe is a bit higher, which is why the overall level maybe is a bit improved, but I believe back in the day if you were good, it showed straight away."

title: 10 things that have happened in F1 before we got GTA 6
excerpt:
Grand Theft Auto 5 was released on September 17th, 2013. After just over 13 years, GTA 6 will finally drop next week.

With that in mind, RacingNews365 has taken a look back at all the things to happen in the F1 world since the last instalment - a time where Sebastian Vettel was in the middle of his then record-breaking nine successive wins, Drive to Survive was something you did when someone was chasing you, and Kimi Antonelli had just celebrated his seventh birthday.

Here are 10 things that happened in F1 before we got GTA 6...

McLaren's rise from the nadir

McLaren went from title contenders to rock bottom, then back to winning titles with the 2024 and 2025 constructors' and 2025 drivers' titles for Norris

After Lewis Hamilton left at the end of 2012, hopes were high at McLaren that Jenson Button would be able to lead the team to the title with an all-new 2013 car.

However, the MP4-28 was badly flawed, and McLaren went through the entire season without a podium, with the rot beginning to set in.

The nadir came between 2015 and 2017 in the Honda years, as poor performances on-track meant a variety of sponsors all jumped ship, leaving the team on its knees, with a boardroom struggle seeing Ron Dennis ousted in 2017.

Enter Zak Brown.

Under Brown's leadership, McLaren has been rebuilt from also-rans to reigning double constructors' titles, with the 2024 success being the first since 1998, and Lando Norris's 2025 title the first of any kind since Hamilton's 2008 crown.

The Mercedes era begins

In 2013, Mercedes was in its fourth season back as a works team, and Hamilton's win in Hungary was just the team's fourth in that time, with no championship success.

Fast forward to today, Mercedes has won 120 more races, is third all-time for most wins, and has claimed a record-breaking eight successive constructors' titles between 2014 and 2021, with seven drivers' titles in that time.

Following a lean spell in ground-effects, it roared back in 2026, with Kimi Antonelli storming to the drivers' crown as it finally regained its constructors' title. At the time of GTA 5's release, Antonelli had just turned seven...

© XPB Images

Ferrari's wait goes on

Since September 2013, Ferrari has gone through five team bosses, seven drivers and won nothing.

Stefano Domenicali, Marco Mattiaci, Maurizio Arrivabene, and Mattia Binotto have all fallen on their swords, with Fred Vasseur currently tasked with returning the team to title-winning ways, which last happened with the 2008 constructors'.

Fernando Alonso, Felipe Massa, Kimi Raikkonen, Sebastian Vettel, Charles Leclerc, Carlos Sainz, and Hamilton have raced full-time for the team since 2013 - with the team recording 28 wins in 13 years.

The closest Ferrari came to a title since was the 2024 constructors', when it fell 14 points short of beating McLaren to the crown.

Half of Alonso's career has passed without a win

Fernando Alonso scored his 32nd career win at the 2013 Spanish GP, which was the 201st race start of his career.

The 2026 São Paulo GP was his 445th start, meaning more than half of his career has passed without the Spanish racer tasting F1 success.

Between 2014 and 2021, he didn't score a podium, although he did not race in 2019 or 2020. After an early-season resurgence with Aston Martin in 2023, he hasn't had another podium since Brazil that year, and given the current plight of Aston Martin, win #33 feels a long way off.

F1's six regulation changes - with another coming

Since 2013, six different eras of F1 cars have been raced.

V8 engines - 2013

Turbo hybrids adopted - 2014

Bigger and more radical aerodynamics - 2017

Major changes to the front wing designs - 2019

Ground effects - 2022

Current rules package - 2026

Another change is on the way with the FIA president Mohammed Ben Sulayem confirming that a change back to V8 engines will happen, likely in 2030.

© XPBimages

F1's stratospheric rise

Back in 2013, F1 was firmly in the vice grip of Bernie Ecclestone, who shunned most forms of social media.

In 2015, things were so bad that talk of three-car teams was even floated, but thankfully, rejected.

In 2017, Liberty Media bought F1 from CVC Capital Partners, and Ecclestone was ousted as CEO, with a new era of social media and openness ushered in.

The best marketing trick was Drive to Survive on Netflix, which opened F1 to new audiences, with social media interactions and the value of teams skyrocketing, with every squad now firmly on a healthy financial footing.

Hamilton's rise

Lewis Hamilton went from a one-time champion with 22 wins to a seven-time champion with 106 wins.

In September 2013, Hamilton was a one-time champion with 22 grand prix wins.

In November 2026, Hamilton is a seven-time champion with 106 grand prix wins.

He is the most successful driver of all time, having rewritten most of the record books during his 12-year stay with Mercedes, which came to an end in 2024 when he defected to join Ferrari.

And Verstappen

Max Verstappen went from karting to a four-time champion with 74 wins.

In 2013, Max Verstappen was in karting and had never driven in a car race.

His debut in single-seaters came in 2014, before becoming the youngest F1 driver of all time at the 2015 Australian GP at just 17 years old.

Fast forward to 2026, he is a four-time world champion, with 75 wins to his name, only behind Hamilton and Michael Schumacher.

In 2023, he won a staggering 19 of 22 races - a record which is likely to stand the test of time.

Nico Hulkenberg!

Nico Hulkenberg got overlooked by all the top teams, changed teams five times, got dropped, came back as a COVID sub, missed a race during that sub spell, returned full-time in 2023 and finally got a podium at the 239th attempt.

Curiously, Nico Hulkenberg was overlooked for a top seat in 2013 and 2014, and moved from Sauber back to Force India for 2014.

He then left for Renault in 2017, got dropped at the end of 2019, before becoming a COVID supersub for Sergio Perez and Lance Stroll in 2020 - but even missed the British GP when subbing for Perez due to an engine problem.

He then subbed for Sebastian Vettel in 2022, before returning full-time in 2023, taking Mick Schumacher's seat at Haas.

For 2025, he changed teams yet again, back to Sauber, in preparation for Audi's takeover for 2026.

At that year's British GP, at the 239th attempt, he finally scored a podium, taking third in a stunning drive on a typically wet Silverstone afternoon.

© XPBimages

Button's grid penalty

Jenson Button raced, retired, came back, got a grid penalty he still hasn't served, and then retired again. Monaco 2017, subbing for Alonso, who was at the Indy 500.

Button was firmly a McLaren man in 2013, still capable of producing results his equipment probably wasn't deserving of, but at the end of 2016, having just reached 300 races, he called time on his career after the Abu Dhabi race.

Or so he thought.

With Alonso racing at the 2017 Indy 500 which clashed with Monaco, Button was drafted in for a one-off appearance, and promptly earned himself a grid penalty for his next race after sending Pascal Wehrlein onto his side at Portier.

Nine years later, Button has still to serve that grid penalty...

© XPBimages

title: F1 drivers react to online abuse change: 'They wouldn't have the balls'
excerpt:
Franco Colapinto and Gabriel Bortoleto have welcomed the FIA's revised online abuse guidelines, insisting the governing body has been "proactive" in tackling a growing problem.

The FIA unveiled its updated Online Community Guidelines alongside its United Against Online Abuse initiative during the São Paulo Grand Prix weekend on November 7, expanding its classification of digital harm into seven categories covering toxic content, impersonation, surveillance and account lockout, among others.

Several F1 drivers have been the subject of severe online abuse this season. Alpine driver Pierre Gasly, his family and girlfriend, are understood to have received 13,000 death threats after the team ordered team-mate Franco Colapinto to let the French driver by during the Spanish Grand Prix.

Incidents with Colapinto, in particular, have often triggered an extreme reaction from his supporters.

Asked for his reaction to the revised guidelines, Colapinto, speaking to the media, including RacingNews365, said: "It's great. I've been fighting really hard against it this year, and I don't want to talk about it much more. I talked enough.

"But generally, it's an area that we have to keep improving as a community, as a sport, in every area, in the world.

"We need to keep an eye on it and keep understanding how we can improve it and just not let it rest.

"We have to be very proactive in the things that we are doing. Me, with the team, with Alpine and everyone in the paddock, we've been fighting really hard against it. Everyone should do so. Let's hope we can keep improving the situation."

[Article continues below]

Bortoleto, speaking alongside Colapinto, pointed to his Alpine rival as having been especially outspoken on the subject this year, before offering his own assessment of the FIA's efforts and the nature of the abuse drivers face.

"The FIA has been doing a very good job on that," said Bortoleto. "And again, I think Franco has been a little bit more openly vocal about it," the Audi driver said.

"I think it's important to be open to constructive criticism because that's okay. We are in a free world. We can listen to opinions, but they need to be constructive.

"They cannot be threatening. They cannot be judging in a negative way because I'm sure these people wouldn't have the balls to do that looking into my eyes or looking into his eyes or anyone's eyes. They do this because they are behind the screen.

"I'm happy if someone wants to come to my face and say something, then it's a different topic. But online abuse, it's for cowards, and I'm sure that the FIA has been taking care of this in a very good way.

"They have been proactive. We have been talking a lot also between the drivers, and I see a lot of progress on that. So hopefully we can keep improving."

The pair's comments come as the FIA has leaned increasingly on technology to police its own channels, deploying automated moderation software such as Arwen.ai to filter abusive comments directed at officials and participants in real time.

The governing body has also built referral pathways with law enforcement through its United Against Online Abuse coalition, aiming to escalate the most serious threats and hate speech for prosecution.

title: Why is Formula E’s new GEN4 regulatory cycle a real F1 scare?
excerpt:
Formula E's new Gen4 race car is set to be unleashed on Monday for the start of pre-season testing. A huge jump to F1 has been made.

As Formula E pre-season testing prepares to get underway on Monday in Madrid, Formula E's new Gen4 car is offering a timely reminder of just how quickly the electric series is closing the performance gap to Formula 1.

Full technical details of the machine, which accelerates harder than an F1 car and matches a Formula 2 car for top speed, have only sharpened that impression, and recent private running has made the comparison look even more pointed to.

The Gen4 car produces a standard race output of 450 kW, around 603 bhp, rising to 600 kW, or roughly 816 bhp, in qualifying trim and when Attack Mode is deployed.

That figure represents a 71 percent jump in peak deployable output over the outgoing Gen3 Evo car, alongside a 43 percent increase in usable battery capacity, now up to 55 kWh.

Those numbers put Gen4 ahead of F2 on paper. The Mecachrome-powered F2 car produces 620 bhp from its single-turbo 3.4-litre V6, noticeably short of Gen4's peak output, despite running in a lighter, rear-wheel-drive configuration.

Formula E's Gen4 reaches 100 km/h in around 1.8 seconds and 200 km/h in 4.4 seconds, comfortably quicker than F2's 2.9 seconds and 6.6 seconds respectively. Top speed is identical at 335 km/h (208 mph), though F2 needs Monza-spec low-downforce aero and DRS to get there.

That theoretical edge has already shown up in practice. Porsche recently conducted a private test at Monza with its development Gen4 car. It reportedly broke Formula 2's lap record there in the process without even attempting a qualifying-style run.

Where Gen4 genuinely embarrasses grand prix machinery is in its drivetrain. The car runs permanent active all-wheel drive, with motors on both axles, something strictly banned under F1's rear-wheel-drive regulations.

Regenerative braking tops out at 700 kW, recovering close to half the energy used in a race, far beyond anything F1's current hybrid system permits. Switchable aero configurations, allowing teams to trim for high downforce or low drag depending on format, add another layer of sophistication once reserved for F1 engineering departments.

First 'legitimate' chance for Formula E versus F1 comparison

Gen4 is not yet an F1 rival on raw numbers. The car weighs around 954 kg without a driver, carries treaded rather than bespoke slick tyres, and its 55 kWh battery limits races to around 45 minutes to an hour, compared to F1's 305-kilometre, sometimes two-hour grands prix.

Formula E teams still rely on lift-and-coast energy management to make it to the flag, whereas F1 deploys its hybrid systems as a performance tool rather than a survival mechanism.

But the trajectory is what matters. Gen4 debuts in 2027 with a season-opener in Mexico City on January 16, almost on an identical layout used by F1. The championship has expanded its calendar to include permanent circuits such as Circuit of The Americas, Brands Hatch and Zandvoort to accommodate the car's increased pace.

The exact lap-time gap between Gen4 and 2026-spec F1 cars on a shared permanent circuit has not yet been measured in competitive conditions, leaving one open question hanging over the entire comparison.

What is no longer in doubt, after Porsche's Monza outing, is that Formula E's all-wheel-drive, high-regeneration electric platform is advancing technologically at a pace that should concern a championship that still, for now, holds every performance card that counts.

"I think Gen4 is such a material step up from where we were with the Gen3 and Gen3 Evo car that perhaps it's the first legitimate point [to be compared to F1]," Formula E CEO Jeff Dodds told RacingNews365.

"It feels like it's the first legitimate chance to showcase the potential of electrified racing. I think the important underlying message is exactly that, which is, this is emerging technology. We all believe in this organisation, it's superior technology, and will become more superior in the future. And Gen4 is a great time to start to showcase that."

title: Toto Wolff draws parallel between Ferrari spat and Lewis Hamilton-Nico Rosberg era
excerpt:
Toto Wolff has said he can "so relate" to what Fred Vasseur is going through at Ferrari with Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc, drawing a direct line to his own experience managing the seven-time F1 champion and Nico Rosberg at Mercedes a decade ago.

The comparison comes after Hamilton and Leclerc clashed on the opening lap of the Mexico City Grand Prix, with Leclerc running across the grass at Turn 4 while disputing the lead, rejoining ahead of his teammate.

In doing so, it demoted Hamilton behind Max Verstappen. Hamilton vented over team radio that Leclerc had pushed him off track, and argued afterwards that the five-second penalty handed to his teammate did nothing to address the imbalance, since Leclerc kept the clean air at the front.

Hamilton's continued pointed comments over the team radio only served to inflame matters, at one stage claiming the team has "big, big problems". The incident sparked a meeting on the following Thursday in São Paulo between Vasseur, Hamilton and Leclerc to clear the air.

Speaking to media, including RacingNews365, Wolff drew a striking parallel to his own management of Hamilton and Rosberg between 2013 and 2016, a four-year spell that ended with Rosberg's retirement days after winning the title.

"Fred doesn't need any advice from me," said Wolff.

"But it's like déjà vu because you've asked me exactly the same question for how many years? 2013, 2014, 2015, 2016, was it? Then Nico called it a day? Four years. Exactly the same situation.

"Sometimes when you put two strong drivers in there, the best ones have edges, and they want to win, and that is a situation that is always very difficult to cope with, obviously under the media spotlight if those cars race at the front.

"So, in that respect, I can so relate to what Fred is going through at the moment."

Asked about Hamilton's radio messages in Mexico City, Wolff suggested such moments can serve a purpose.

"Sometimes it needs the really tough ones to make a point," he said.

"With Nico and Lewis, when there was an accident, it was understood that that was now the limit, and it wouldn't continue like this.

"That's why, maybe, it needed to escalate to that point, because it's respect for the team, the many thousands of people, the brand, who work together, and that's what they need to keep in their heads."

title: George Russell faced with Nico Rosberg-Daniel Ricciardo F1 career crossroads
excerpt:
George Russell is faced with a defining juncture in his F1 career that could go "one of two ways" - either that of Nico Rosberg or Daniel Ricciardo.

That's the verdict of Sky Sports F1 pundit and analyst Karun Chandhok, who is wondering in which direction Russell will head after being "pretty beaten up" this year by Mercedes team-mate Kimi Antonelli.

Chandhok feels Russell could follow the path of Rosberg, who bounced back in 2016 to become F1 champion after witnessing the rise of Lewis Hamilton at Mercedes the previous two years as the British driver won the second and third of his seven titles overall.

Or, Russell may find himself following in the footsteps of Daniel Ricciardo, who eventually found himself overwhelmed by rising star Max Verstappen at Red Bull and opted to leave, sparking the beginning of the end of his F1 journey.

Chandhok framed the next year or so as pivotal for the Briton.

"Here's an interesting one for George Russell, and I'm fascinated to see what happens over the next 15 months between now and the end of next season," he said.

"It can go one of two ways [for him]: either George Russell can do a Nico Rosberg and go from 2015 to 2016 and make a step up and take the fight for the world championship, and win the world championship in the following year, having been pretty beaten up this year.

"Or he could end up in a Daniel Ricciardo situation where he was the established number one in the team, had this young pup Max Verstappen arrive, a generational talent in that Red Bull team, and in the end, he opted to leave.

"He thought, 'You know what, I can't beat this guy, so I'm going to go somewhere else and go for Renault'.

"Does he end up in that scenario where he suddenly realises over the next 15 months, 'No, this is not happening for me. I can't beat this kid in this team, and I've got to start thinking about something else'.

"I'm interested to see which one he ends up following."

[Article continues below]

Mexico summed up Russell season

Russell's title-challenging defeat to Antonelli was confirmed at the recent Mexico City Grand Prix as the 20-year-old Italian became the youngest champion in F1 history.

The 28-year-old has said that his season has been beset with issues which have exhausted him, pointing to the fact he had had just six clean weekends all year.

Chandhok was careful to note, though, that Russell's defeat to Antonelli this season has not been purely down to misfortune.

"He has had more issues than his teammate, there's no questioning that," said Chandhok.

"But by his own admission, he's also not been as fast as his teammate. So I think Kimi Antonelli has won the championship because he's been the faster Mercedes driver, and Mercedes produced the fastest car across the season.

"And I think he's won the championship this early in the season, because George Russell has had more bad luck than he has."

Pointing to the most recent round in Mexico, Chandhok singled out the weekend as symbolic of his campaign.

"That weekend just summed it up for him," he remarked.

"He started on the front row, had an engine issue, didn't have power on the opening lap, and all of a sudden he finds himself down in fifth, sixth place.

"It was a frustrating race, just stuck in traffic. It just summed up his weekend, summed up his season, really."
